title: Cadets being told to stand down as Canada spends billions on defence
summary: The Canadian military has suspended most weekend cadet training and competitions in parts of the country until March, citing budget restraint. Leaked emails reveal mounting financial pressures…

image.caption: Cadets march in a parade following a Remembrance Day ceremony in New Brunswick. Cadets in Ontario and B.C. are facing cutbacks as the Department of National Defence works to hit budget reduction targets. (Darren Calabrese/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

The Canadian military has suspended most weekend cadet training and competitions in parts of the country until March, citing budget restraint. Leaked emails reveal mounting financial pressures despite billions in new defence spending.
Budget restraint sidelines youth training despite Ottawa's massive investments
The Canadian military has put a halt to most cadet training in various parts of the country because of ongoing budget restraint within the Department of National Defence.
The halt involves weekend training and participation in competitions and will last until the end of the fiscal year in March. Weekly parade nights, however, will continue at least for the time being.

A series of internal emails, obtained by CBC News, outline the decision and paint a picture of an organization struggling to manage the impact of the Defence Department's cuts to operations and support funding.
The Ottawa Citizen was the first to report on the restrictions involving the cadet program. The news was confirmed by a subsequent leak of emails to CBC News.

items: Billions more for defence, but Canada's military still faces an old budget squeeze

blocks.text: "Due to the current fiscal environment, all cadet activities are paused for the remainder of the current fiscal year, ending 31 March 2027, with the exception of weekly parade nights, which may continue at this time," said one leaked email quoting Lt.-Col. Raphael MacKenzie, who commands Ontario's Regional Cadet Support Unit (Central).
No one at the Defence Department was immediately available to comment on the leaked documents.
In mid-October, CBC News was the first to report on the department's internal belt-tightening, which is a knock-on effect from cuts mandated in previous federal budgets.
Department expected to find $459M in savings

The Defence Department has been given tens of billions of new funding by the government of Prime Minister Mark Carney. It has been told to focus that extra cash on priority areas, including the purchase of much-needed combat equipment.
At the same time, DND is subject to the demand for operations and maintenance reductions announced by the Trudeau government in 2023 and enacted in the 2024 federal budget.
Those reductions, according to the latest federal budget, are significant.
DND is expected to find $459 million in operational savings this fiscal year, and another $459 million next year.
Last week, CBC News reported on how a reserve unit in southwestern Ontario limited paid participation in Remembrance Day activities because of the budget restraint.
There are also unconfirmed reports of full-time reservists having their three-year contracts cancelled with less than 30 days' notice.
That runs contrary to the latest federal budget's departmental plans report, which downplayed the impact of the internal restraint.
"No job losses are anticipated as a result of these reductions," said the budget report, recently tabled in Parliament.

The department and the Canadian military remain in "a period of growth, supported by significant long-term defence investments that continue to strengthen operational readiness, capabilities and the civilian and military workforce needed to deliver them," the report said.
Defence will enter the 'top rank' of government spending: PBO

Conservative defence critic James Bezan said the reserves and cadets are bearing the brunt of the restraint and the budget chaos makes a mockery of the Liberal government's pledge to invest in defence.
"Mark Carney and the Liberals can't be talking out of both sides of their mouths, saying that they're investing in the armed forces and then cutting operations," Bezan said.
"That reduces our readiness. The Carney cuts are having real impacts on the day-to-day operations of the Canadian Armed Forces."
The restrictions on cadet activities took effect immediately in Ontario, while similar measures will come into force on Nov. 21 in British Columbia.

items: Military budget squeeze limits paid Remembrance Day participation in Ontario

blocks.text: A separate email detailing the restraint in the B.C. region said that cadet leadership is trying to preserve activities that directly support the conduct of weekly training at corps and squadrons and that remains "our priority."
The commanding officer of the Pacific region plans to conduct town halls on Nov. 19 and Nov. 23 to further explain the decision.

"We recognize that this direction will come as a surprise to most and will be disappointing to cadets, families and your teams who have invested considerable time and effort in planning activities for the year ahead," said the second email, dated Nov. 16.
"We share that disappointment. These are not measures that would be taken if the resources were available to sustain the program as planned."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.
